title: Reinforcement Learning with Discrete Diffusion Policies for Combinatorial Action Spaces
claim: Learning proceeds as an iterative loop: evaluate the policy, build a regularized target, then fit an expressive model to it by distribution matching.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right chain of boxes, feedback loop returning underneath
description: A single horizontal flowchart read left to right. It starts with a yellow oval, 'Collect Data', which sends data D into a blue 'Policy Evaluation' box. That box feeds an orange parallelogram for the Q-function q^{π_k}. An arrow labelled 'Construct via Eq. (3)' leads to a green 'PMD Target' box, π_MD^k. The target goes to a blue 'Minimize Loss' box that holds the objective min over π_θ of E[d(π_θ, π_MD^k; s)]. A blue 'Discrete Diffusion Model' box sits above it, with an arrow labelled 'Parameterize π_θ'. The output is an orange parallelogram, 'New Policy' π_{k+1}. A long return arrow runs along the bottom back to Collect Data, labelled 'Next Iteration (k ← k+1)'. Colors mark the type of element: blue for processes, orange for quantities, green for the target. The eye starts at the oval on the left.
caption: {Overview of the RL-D$^2$ Framework. Our framework adopts a policy iteration structure. Following policy evaluation, which estimates the current Q-function, the policy improvement step is implemented as a distributional matching problem. Here, the discrete diffusion policy is trained to minimize the KL divergence (FKL or RKL) relative to an optimal target distribution ($\pi_{MD}^k$) derived via Policy Mirror Descent in [ref].}
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) struggles to scale to large, combinatorial action spaces common in many real-world problems. This paper introduces a novel framework for training discrete diffusion models as highly effective policies in these complex settings. Our key innovation is an efficient online training process that ensures stable and effective policy improvement. By leveraging policy mirror descent (PMD) to define an ideal, regularized target policy distribution, we frame the policy update as a distributional matching problem, training the expressive diffusion model to replicate this stable target. This decoupled approach stabilizes learning and significantly enhances training performance. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results and superior sample efficiency across a diverse set of challenging combinatorial benchmarks, including DNA sequence generation, RL with macro-actions, and multi-agent systems. Experiments demonstrate that our diffusion policies attain superior performance compared to other baselines.
